10.1016/j.intimp.2024.112574.scope: Full-article-supported candidate-gene and mouse-expression evidence. Unresolved human cohort accounting and model-validation questions prevent a complete V2 upgrade.

sections.heading: Five candidate genes and experimental follow-up
sections.text: The article selects DLST, ATP7B, FDX1, SLC31A1 and DLAT after a retrospective public-transcriptomic analysis. The full text is now available for review, but its classification performance is not treated here as independently validated clinical diagnosis.
sections.source_locator: Publisher-layout PDF pp. 2–3, Methods 2.1–2.5; pp. 5–8, Results 3.3 and Figures 4–5.

sections.heading: Mouse expression evidence
sections.text: Methods 2.9 describes male C57BL/6 mice assigned to sham control or left-anterior-descending coronary artery ligation, six per group. Figure 8 reports echocardiography with n=6 and Western blot with n=4; these are separate reported assay counts, not additional animal cohorts. The myocardial Western blot and immunohistochemistry show higher DLST and ATP7B and lower FDX1, SLC31A1 and DLAT in the ligation group. This establishes reported expression differences in the tested model, not that these genes cause cuproptosis or diagnose disease in patients.
sections.source_locator: Publisher-layout PDF pp. 3–4, Methods 2.9–2.14; p. 8, Results 3.6; p. 11, Figure 8C–E and caption (echocardiography n=6; Western blot n=4).

sections.heading: Computational chemical hypotheses
sections.text: Chemical–gene associations were retrieved from CTD and examined with molecular docking. These analyses generate hypotheses; no compound-treatment experiment or human treatment benefit is established by this article.
sections.source_locator: Publisher-layout PDF p. 3, Methods 2.8; pp. 8 and 10, Results 3.5 and Figure 7; pp. 3–4, animal experimental methods.

sections.heading: Why diagnostic validation remains unresolved
sections.text: Figure 1 labels the training inputs as 181 IC samples from GSE5406 and 91 from GSE57338, but labels their merged IC group as 203. Those counts do not reconcile. Moreover, GSE57338 is a SubSeries of the stated validation accession GSE57345; the article does not provide a verified sample-level exclusion map. Figure 5 describes five-fold cross-validation within its evaluation datasets. These records do not establish an untouched external test of a frozen diagnostic model.
sections.source_locator: Official GEO Series GSE57338, relation “SubSeries of: GSE57345”; compare publisher PDF p. 3 Figure 1, p. 2 Methods 2.1 and p. 8 Figure 5 caption.

limitations: Human sample accounting remains unresolved: Figure 1 input IC counts 181 and 91 do not equal the displayed combined 203. No corrected denominator or deduplicated participant total is inferred. The GSE42955 AUC is 0.943 in the abstract but 0.933 in Results 3.3 and Figure 5D. Neither number is selected as a reconciled performance estimate.

Training GSE57338 is part of validation SuperSeries GSE57345. A GSM-level membership and overlap audit and the frozen-model evaluation procedure are needed before claiming independent external validation. The article alternates between disease identification and cluster prediction. Methods 2.4, Results 3.3 and the Figure 5 caption do not resolve the exact target and partitioning of every model analysis.

Animal expression differences do not demonstrate causal cuproptosis activity, clinical diagnostic utility or treatment efficacy. The post-ligation assessment interval and the relationship between the six allocated animals and four Western-blot observations require clarification.
Supplementary Figures S1–S7 and Tables S1–S3 were not obtained in this review. No supplementary-only values or docking-based therapeutic recommendation is adopted.
The author-account PDF matches the formal article title, DOI, 18-author order, journal, volume and article number. It is retained privately for audit; no open redistribution licence is asserted.

sections.text: The acquired document is the publisher-typeset advance article first published on 18 December 2024, with 10 authors and DOI 10.1093/hmg/ddae189. The publisher subsequently assigned volume 34, issue 5, pages 381–391 in 2025. The complete article, supplementary figures, supplementary tables and STROBE-MR checklist are available for this review. sections.heading: Blood and brain expression context
sections.text: The study reports separate transcriptomic comparisons using blood dataset GSE63061 (139 Alzheimer’s disease cases and 134 controls) and brain dataset GSE33000 (310 cases and 157 controls). It constructs a senescence-related expression score from upregulated and downregulated gene sets, then integrates expression and methylation QTL with GWAS summary data. An expression-based score is not a direct count of senescent cells; these retrospective comparisons do not establish a treatment effect.
sections.source_locator: Advance-article PDF pp. 2–3, Results: Analysis of cellular senescence features in AD; p. 8, Materials and methods: Data collection and Processing; supplementary_table_ddae189.xlsx, Supplementary Table 9 gene sets and Supplementary Table 10 rows 3–5.

sections.heading: Unresolved analysis-input version
sections.text: The article Methods and Supplementary Table 10 identify FinnGen R9 G6_ALZHEIMER and report 9,301 cases with 367,976 controls. The official R9 Risteys endpoint independently confirms 9,301 cases after genotype quality control. However, STROBE-MR item 4d reports 7,759 cases and 334,740 controls under the same R9 label. The available materials do not identify the exact outcome input file used in the reported MR runs. The official R9 case count is known; the unresolved issue is which input generated this paper’s estimates. No disputed denominator is selected and no full V2 genetic conclusion is certified.
sections.source_locator: PDF p. 8, GWAS data for Alzheimer’s disease; supplementary_table_ddae189.xlsx, Supplementary Table 10 row 6; supplementary_materials_ddae189.docx, STROBE-MR item 4d. Official cross-check: R9 Risteys G6_ALZHEIMER, Case counts → Remove individuals based on genotype QC (linked in Provenance).

sections.heading: Cell-line follow-up and its limits
sections.text: The Methods describe PC12 cells exposed to 7 μM Aβ1–42 for 12 hours. Figure 4E–G and the supplementary expression records report higher CDKN2B and ITGAV expression in treated cells than in controls. This is a cell-line expression comparison, not evidence from human Alzheimer’s disease neurons or a demonstration of therapeutic benefit. Because the plotted qPCR scale and supplementary values are inconsistent, this note does not certify an exact fold change or plotted significance value.
sections.source_locator: PDF p. 9, Cell culture and Aβ1–42-induced AD modeling and RNA isolation, reverse transcription, and quantitative real-time PCR; Figure 4E–G; supplementary_table_ddae189.xlsx, sheets labelled Supplemenatry Table 7 (B3:C6, B9:C12) and Supplemenatry Table 8; Supplementary Figures 5–6.

limitations: Full V2 remains on hold until an exact archived GWAS input filename/release and checksum, linked to the analysis code or run record, or a formal author clarification resolves which dataset generated the MR estimates. Agreement between the main Methods and the official R9 case count does not establish the analysis input used.

The source contains unresolved mediation annotations: Figure 1 labels an EXOSC9 probe differently from Table 1/Figure 3C, and Figure 3 coefficients differ from the MR tables, including a SLFN12 sign discrepancy. This note neither corrects the labels nor certifies the proposed mediation chains.

The qPCR supplement lists four values per group per target and the immunoblot supplement lists three entries per group; biological independence is not specified. The qPCR plot/table scale discrepancy remains unresolved, so no exact fold change, effective biological sample size or plotted P value is certified.

MR depends on instrument relevance, independence and exclusion restriction. The reported sensitivity checks do not prove all assumptions, and the supplement reports significant SLFN12 heterogeneity. Gene-target causality is not established by this limited note.

The PC12 experiments measure expression after an amyloid-peptide challenge. They do not test gene knockdown or rescue, animal disease modification, patient outcomes, or the safety and efficacy of a treatment. An ambiguous CDKN2B primer character and absent GAPDH primer sequence in Supplementary Table 11 also limit reproducibility.

sections.heading: Principal findings
sections.text: Vesicles released by ZFP36-overexpressing AC16 cells protected RSL3-challenged human umbilical vein endothelial cells: viability and mitochondrial membrane potential improved, while oxidative stress declined. Direct myocardial administration also improved cardiac function and reduced fibrosis in a mouse infarction model.
sections.source_locator: Sections 3.3–3.4 and Figures 3–4, pages 6–7 and 9–10; endothelial stress assays and post-infarction outcomes.

sections.heading: Vascular-interface contribution
sections.text: ZFP36-engineered vesicles were immobilized on polydopamine/hyaluronic-acid-modified NiTi. The coating had a particle-based loading efficiency of 72.80% ± 0.83% (mean ± SD, n=3) and released NTA-detected particles over 14 days in PBS. In the rat femoral-artery injury model, the coated filaments supported endothelial recovery and reduced local inflammatory and lipid-peroxidation-associated signals.

sections.text: The cell challenge addresses endothelial protection; the mouse infarction model tests intramyocardial delivery; the rat injury model tests the local vascular interface. 10.1177/00368504261499186.scope: Original author-maintained explanation of an observational mortality analysis in CKM stages 0–3, based on the indexed abstract and verified publication metadata.

sections.heading: Research question and design
sections.text: The study examined whether EASIX was associated with later mortality among 10,885 NHANES participants aged at least 30 years with cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome stages 0–3. It retrospectively analyzed survey cycles from 1999–2018, linking deaths through 2019. EASIX is calculated as lactate dehydrogenase multiplied by creatinine, divided by platelet count.
sections.source_locator: PubMed PMID 42893432, Abstract Objective and Methods: population, NHANES cycles, mortality linkage and EASIX definition.

sections.heading: Principal quantitative findings
sections.text: Over a median 97 months of follow-up, 1,122 participants died; 295 deaths were cardiovascular. Per one-unit higher EASIX, the adjusted hazard ratio was 1.41 (95% CI 1.24–1.61) for all-cause mortality and 1.30 (95% CI 1.13–1.49) for cardiovascular mortality. The abstract reports that the associations persisted after further lifestyle adjustment.
sections.source_locator: PubMed PMID 42893432, Abstract Results: follow-up, deaths, adjusted HRs and CIs, one-unit exposure scale and lifestyle adjustment.

sections.heading: Scientific contribution and use
sections.text: The analysis connects a composite endothelial-stress index with long-term outcomes among adults at CKM stages 0–3. It provides an observational comparator for epidemiologic discussions of endothelial stress, CKM staging and mortality; survey-weighted Cox models and spline analyses supply the reported association framework. Clinical risk-assessment use requires further validation.
sections.source_locator: PubMed PMID 42893432, Abstract Methods and Conclusions: survey-weighted Cox models, restricted cubic splines, CKM stage scope and risk-assessment interpretation.

sections.heading: Principal contribution
sections.text: This review connects biomedical data provenance and endpoint design with model selection, causal interpretation, validation, and deployment governance. Its disease-agnostic framework includes an evidence ladder for positioning AI findings and a proposed model-and-data card for reproducible reporting. It synthesizes methods across omics, imaging/pathology, clinical records, and longitudinal data to guide trustworthy research and translation.

sections.heading: Evidence ladder
sections.text: The review organizes support for an AI finding into association, robustness, biological coherence, causal support, perturbation evidence, and clinical utility. The ladder helps researchers identify what additional evidence is needed to move a finding toward a biological explanation or clinical application.
sections.source_locator: Evidence ladder, manuscript lines 491–518, physical PDF pages 26–27.

sections.heading: Research use
sections.text: The framework can inform the design and reporting of studies that combine biomedical data types. Its proposed model-and-data card gives researchers a place to document data provenance, model choices and validation conditions alongside the intended use.
